title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: "Yes, there is something in me that's hateful, repulsive," Levin thought as he left the Shtcherbatskys' and walked toward his brother's lodgings. "And I don't get on with other people. Pride, they say. No, I have no pride. If I had any pride, I wouldn't have put myself in such a position." And he pictured Vronsky to himself, happy, good-natured, clever, self-possessed, certainly never put in the awful position he had been in that evening. "Yes, she was bound to choose him. That's how it had to be, and I have no one and nothing to blame. I'm the one to blame. What right did I have to imagine she would care to join her life with mine? Who am I and what am I? A nobody, not wanted by anyone or useful to anybody." And he remembered his brother Nikolay, and dwelt with pleasure on the thought of him. "Isn't he right that everything in the world is base and loathsome? And are we fair in our judgment of brother Nikolay? Of course, from Prokofy's point of view, seeing him in a torn cloak and tipsy, he's a despicable person. But I know him differently. I know his soul, and I know that we're like him. And I, instead of going to find him, went out to dinner, and came here." Levin walked up to a lamppost, read his brother's address from his pocketbook, and called a sledge. The whole long way to his brother's, Levin vividly recalled all the facts of his brother Nikolay's life that were familiar to him. He remembered how at the university, and for a year afterward, his brother had, despite the mockery of his companions, lived like a monk, strictly observing all religious rites, services, and fasts, and avoiding every kind of pleasure, especially women. And how afterward he had broken out all at once: had run with the most horrible people, plunged into the most senseless debauchery. He remembered the later scandal over a boy whom he had brought from the country to bring up, and, in a fit of rage, had beaten so violently that proceedings were brought against him for unlawful wounding. Then he remembered the scandal with a sharper to whom he had lost money and given a promissory note, and against whom he had himself lodged a complaint, claiming he had cheated him. (This was the money Sergey Ivanovitch had paid.) Then he remembered the night he had spent in the lockup for disorderly conduct in the street. He remembered the shameful proceedings he had tried to bring against his brother Sergey Ivanovitch, accusing him of not having paid him his share of their mother's fortune, and the latest scandal — when he had gone to a western province in an official capacity and got into trouble for assaulting a village elder... It was all horribly disgusting, and yet to Levin it appeared in nothing like the disgusting light it inevitably would to those who did not know Nikolay, did not know his whole story, did not know his heart.

Levin remembered that when Nikolay had been in his devout phase — the period of fasts and monks and church services, when he had been looking to religion for a support and a curb for his passionate nature — far from encouraging him, everyone, including Levin himself, had jeered at him. They had teased him, called him Noah and the monk; and when he had broken out, no one had helped him, but everyone had turned away from him with horror and disgust.

Levin felt that, in spite of all the ugliness of his life, his brother Nikolay, in his soul, in the very depths of his soul, was no more in the wrong than the people who despised him. He was not to blame for having been born with his unbridled temperament and his somehow limited intelligence. But he had always wanted to be good. "I'll tell him everything, hold nothing back, and I'll make him speak openly to me too, and I'll show him that I love him and so understand him," Levin resolved to himself, as he reached the hotel he had the address of, around eleven o'clock.
"At the top, 12 and 13," the porter answered Levin's inquiry.
"At home?"
"Sure to be at home."

The door of No. 12 was half open, and out into the streak of light came thick fumes of cheap, poor tobacco and the sound of a voice unknown to Levin; but he knew at once that his brother was there — he heard his cough.
As he went in the door, the unknown voice was saying:
"It all depends with how much judgment and knowledge the thing's done."

Konstantin Levin looked in at the door, and saw that the speaker was a young man with an enormous shock of hair wearing a Russian jerkin, and that a pockmarked woman in a woolen gown, without collar or cuffs, was sitting on the sofa. His brother was not in sight. Konstantin felt a sharp pang at his heart at the thought of the strange company in which his brother spent his life. No one had heard him, and Konstantin, taking off his galoshes, listened to what the man in the jerkin was saying. He was talking about some sort of enterprise.
"Well, the devil take them, the privileged classes," his brother's voice responded, with a cough. "Masha! Get us some supper and some wine if any's left; if not, go and get some."
The woman got up, came out from behind the screen, and saw Konstantin.
"There's some gentleman here, Nikolay Dmitrievitch," she said.
"Whom do you want?" said Nikolay Levin's voice, angrily.
"It's me," answered Konstantin Levin, stepping forward into the light.

"Who's _me?_" Nikolay's voice asked again, even angrier. He could be heard getting up hurriedly, stumbling against something, and Levin saw, facing him in the doorway, the big, scared eyes and huge, thin, stooping figure of his brother — so familiar and yet astonishing in its weirdness and sickliness.

He had grown even thinner than three years ago, when Konstantin Levin had last seen him. He was wearing a short coat, and his hands and big bones looked larger than ever. His hair had thinned, the same straight mustaches covered his lips, the same eyes stared strangely and naïvely at his visitor.

"Ah, Kostya!" he exclaimed suddenly, recognizing his brother, and his eyes lit up with joy. But the same second he glanced at the young man and gave that nervous jerk of his head and neck Konstantin knew so well, as though his neckband were hurting him; and a quite different expression — wild, suffering, cruel — settled on his emaciated face.
"I wrote to you and Sergey Ivanovitch both that I don't know you and don't want to know you. What is it you want?"

He was nothing like what Konstantin had been picturing. The worst and most tiresome side of his character — what made all relations with him so difficult — had been forgotten by Konstantin Levin when he thought of him, and now, seeing his face, and especially that nervous twitching of his head, he remembered it all.
"I didn't want to see you for anything," he answered timidly. "I've simply come to see you."
His brother's timidity obviously softened Nikolay. His lips twitched.

"Oh, so that's it?" he said. "Well, come in, sit down. Like some supper? Masha, bring supper for three. No, wait. Do you know who this is?" he said, addressing his brother and pointing to the man in the jerkin. "This is Mr. Kritsky, a friend of mine from Kiev, a very remarkable man. The police are after him, of course, because he's not a scoundrel."

And he looked round the room the way he always did at everyone in it. Seeing that the woman standing in the doorway was about to leave, he shouted at her, "Wait a minute, I said." And with the inability to express himself, the incoherence that Konstantin knew so well, he began, with another look round at everyone, to tell his brother Kritsky's story: how he had been expelled from the university for starting a benefit society for poor students and Sunday schools; how he had then been a teacher in a peasant school, had been driven out of that too, and had afterward been tried for something.
"You're from Kiev university?" Konstantin Levin said to Kritsky, to break the awkward silence that followed.
"Yes, I was at Kiev," Kritsky replied angrily, his face darkening.

"And this woman," Nikolay Levin cut in, pointing to her, "is the partner of my life, Marya Nikolaevna. I took her out of a bad house" — and he jerked his neck as he said it — "but I love her and respect her, and anyone who wants to know me," he added, raising his voice and knitting his brows, "I ask to love her and respect her too. She's just the same as my wife, just the same. So now you know whom you have to deal with. And if you think you're lowering yourself, well, there's the floor, there's the door."
And again his eyes traveled inquiringly over them all.
"Why I should be lowering myself, I don't understand."
"Then, Masha, tell them to bring supper; three portions, spirits and wine... No, wait... No, it doesn't matter... Go on."
